CONGRANT.TITLE: 2021 MSEIP – Long-Range Improvement of Retention and Success Rates for UTRGV Hispanic Electrical and Computer Engineering Students
Improving Spectrum Efficiency in Battleground MANETs
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This project investigates improving the spectrum efficiency in battleground mobile adhoc networks (MANETs) with dynamic spectrum access (DSA). To achieve informationdominance in battlegrounds, one key is the ability to efficiently use the electromagneticspectrum. Cognitive radio (CR) and DSA are innovative ways to improving spectrum efficiencyin communications. Although experiments have been done on the potentials of DSA inbattlegrounds, many challenges still need to be addressed before DSA can really perform inbattlegrounds. One such challenge is fast, accurate, and engery-efficient spectrum sensing inbattlegrounds, and another is fast rendezvousing of battle units in a radio channel that is sensedavailable at a given time. Because of the highly dynamic spectrum activities in a battleground,DSA with slow or inaccurate spectrum sensing or slow rendezvousing will be impractical in abattleground. Most existing spectrum sensing and rendezvousing schemes are designed targetingcivil networks, and are not suitable for battleground MANETs because of their inaccuracy,latency, or energy consumption. Our basic approach to the spectrum sensing and rendezvousingchallenges in battleground MANETs is spectrum access assistance (SAA) based on primitiveasynchronous communication. With our knowledge on priority scheduling in MANETs usingprimitive tone-based communication, in this project we will investigate fast, accurate, andenergy-efficient spectrum sensing that incorporates SAA from primary users (PUs). Based on thesame approach, we will also investigate fast rendezvousing that allows battle units in abattleground to quickly rendezvous in a radio channel.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Network State Conservation in Systems with Spectrum Coexistence
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
CNS Core: Small: RUI: Network State Conservation in Systems with Spectrum Coexistence
Project Summary
Overview: The proliferation of wireless devices has been straining the limited radio spectrum in recent years. The spectrum shortage problem will deteriorate as the ideas of Internet of things and smart communities are gaining acceptance. Spectrum coexistence becomes one important approach to improving spectrum efficiency. In systems with spectrum coexistence, communication and networking protocols need to coexist and collaborate to make spectrum constantly busy. This project investigates methods improving protocol efficiency for secondary users in spectrum coexistence systems. One important direction of the investigation is the impact of a cognitive-radio physical layer on the upper layers, such as the medium access control sub-layer and the transport layer. A cognitive-radio physical layer coupled with dynamic spectrum access may interrupt the activities at an upper layer at any given time, which can be costly in terms of spectral and energy efficiency. For example, when a cognitive-radio physical layer interrupts the ACK transmission in a RTS-CTS-DATA-ACK cycle of the IEEE 802.11 DCF, the energy and spectrum used for accomplishing the RTS-CTS-DATA exchange are totally wasted, impairing both spectral and energy efficiency in the network. This type of waste of resources may also occur in other protocols and at other upper layers in a spectrum coexistence system. For example, a smoothly running TCP cycle may be terminated by the cognitive-radio physical layer, resulting in otherwise successful data packets being retransmitted. On one hand, a secondary user must vacate a band as soon as the primary user needs it. On the other hand, a secondary user may waste a significant amount of energy and spectrum when it abruptly terminates its current or scheduled transmission and thus disrupts a  protocol cycle. The proposed project investigates the spectral and energy impact of a cognitive-radio physical layer on the upper layers, and propose new network architectures and protocols to reduce or avoid such impact in spectrum coexistence systems.  
Intellectual merit: The proposed project investigates methods improving the protocol efficiency for secondary users in spectrum coexistence systems. Existing methods usually rely on the prediction of  primary user’s traffic patterns in improving the protocol efficiency for secondary users, but it is intrinsically difficult to predict the primary user’s traffic arrivals and the duration of each arrival. Instead of relying on predicting the primary user’s traffic patterns, this project, based on protocol state conservation, redesigns the protocols of the secondary users to minimize the impact of the primary user on the secondary users. In addition, this project uses cross-layer collaboration in improving the protocol efficiency for secondary users. Although the basic approach of cross-layer design is not new in communications and networking research, the coupling of spectrum access assistance with state conservation across layers is a new method for improving spectral and energy efficiency in spectrum coexistence systems. In the implementation of this new method, new network architectures and protocols will need to be investigated, and new insights will be discovered in dynamic spectrum access in terms of spectral and energy efficiency.    
Broader impacts: The proposed project will benefit the society as a whole as well as some underrepresented minority groups in STEM. Spectrum and energy are two types of resources that are critical to a modern society. The spectrum resource becomes more strained every day, while pollution from energy consumption causes serious problems for the environment. The proposed project will improve both spectral and energy efficiency in wireless networks which are becoming ubiquitous. The proposed project will save a significant amount of energy consumed by future wireless networks. The saved energy will reduce emissions from electricity generation and benefit the environment. Besides its likely significant impact on the society as a whole, the project will promote STEM education among minority groups with its hiring and training of underrepresented minority students in STEM. The majority of students at UTRGV are Hispanics, who are underrepresented in STEM. We will actively recruit Hispanic students on the campus in the project. Our recruiting efforts will be facilitated by the resources available at UTRGV, such as the ADVANCE program funded by NSF and the Office of Engaged Scholarship & Learning, both of which promote STEM education for Hispanics. 
Key words: [Wireless Networks][Network Protocols][Performance, Spectrum Coexistence][Dynamic Spectrum Access]

CONGRANT.TITLE: A New Form of Antenna Diversity for Improved Spectral and Energy Efficiency in Wireless Networks
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
It is well-known that antenna diversity techniques, ranging from simple antenna switching to highly optimized multiple input - multiple output systems, substantially improve the reliability and capacity of wireless communications. Typical forms of antenna diversity are spatial, pattern, and polarization diversity. We propose a new diversity method, antenna impulse response diversity (AIRD), which uses
multiple co-located antennas that have direction-dependent impulse responses. Preliminary work suggests that the new method has many of the advantages of spatial diversity without the need for an electrically large footprint. In contrast with pattern diversity, the new approach uses omnidirectional
patterns which maintain large diversity gain in multicast applications limited by the weakest peer. In its simplest form using selection diversity, AIRD can work with any transceiver architecture without modification, and consumes negligible additional power. Most importantly for the SpecEES program
objectives of spectral efficiency and energy efficiency, antenna diversity reduces the transmit power required to obtain a given quality of service, thus lowering the ambient interference level and increasing availability for all users of the spectrum.

We propose to (a) develop multiport antennas suitable for AIRD, (b) fully characterize the performance in multipath fields, (c) evaluate performance in realistic wireless networks through both multilayer network modeling and field tests using both measurement grade and standard commercial wireless network adapters, (d) produce publicly available performance data, antenna designs, and models suitable for system level design. The project team is a collaboration of two specialists, one in wireless network protocols, and one in electromagnetics and antenna design.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Dynamic Spectrum Access in Battleground MANETs
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
In this project we investigate dynamic spectrum access (DSA) in battleground mobile ad-
hoc networks (MANETs). For achieving information dominance in battlegrounds, one key is the
ability to innovatively use the electromagnetic spectrum. Cognitive radio (CR) and DSA have
been proposed as innovative ways to improve spectrum efficiency in communications. Although
experiments have been done on the potentials of DSA in battlegrounds, many challenges still
need to be addressed before DSA can really perform in battlegrounds. One such challenge is fast,
accurate, and energy-efficient spectrum sensing in battlegrounds, and another is fast
rendezvousing of battle units in a radio channel that is sensed available at a given time. Due to
the highly dynamic spectrum activities in a battleground, DSA with slow or inaccurate spectrum
sensing or slow rendezvousing will be ineffective. Existing spectrum sensing and rendezvousing
schemes are designed, in general, targeting civil networks, and are not suitable for battleground
MANETs because of their inaccuracy, latency, or energy consumption. Our basic approach to the
spectrum sensing and rendezvousing challenges in battleground MANETs is spectrum access
assistance (SAA) based on primitive asynchronous communication. With our knowledge on
priority scheduling in MANETs using primitive tone-based communication, in this project we
will investigate fast, accurate, and energy-efficient spectrum sensing that incorporates SAA from
primary users (PUs). Based on the same approach, we will also investigate fast rendezvousing
that allows battle units in a battleground to quickly rendezvous in a radio channel.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Network State Conservation in Dynamic Spectrum Access
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Overview:
The proposed project is on improving spectral and energy efficiency in dynamic spectrum access via
cross-layer collaboration. The proliferation of wireless devices has been straining the limited radio
spectrum in recent years, particularly in heavily populated areas. The spectrum shortage problem will
deteriorate as the ideas of Internet of things and smart communities are starting to gain attention and
acceptance. Although cognitive radio and dynamic spectrum access may alleviate the spectrum shortage
problem, they may aggravate the energy shortage problem of wireless devices powered by batteries due
to the required constant channel sensing. Simultaneously addressing spectral efficiency and energy
efficiency in dynamic spectrum access is thus critical. One perspective to this problem is to study the
impact of a cognitive-radio physical layer on the upper layers, such as the medium access control sub-
layer. A cognitive-radio physical layer coupled with dynamic spectrum access may interrupt the activities
at an upper layer at any given time, which can be costly in terms of spectral and energy efficiency. For
example, when a cognitive-radio physical layer interrupts the ACK transmission in a RTS-CTS-DATA-
ACK cycle of the IEEE 802.11 DCF, the energy and spectrum used for accomplishing the RTS-CTS-
DATA exchange are totally wasted, impairing both spectral and energy efficiency in the network. If this
type of energy and spectrum waste caused by a cognitive-radio physical layer can be reduced or avoided,
the spectral and energy efficiency in the cognitive radio network will significantly improve, as shown by
the data in the proposal. On one hand, a secondary user must vacate a band as soon as the primary user
needs it. On the other hand, a secondary user may waste significant energy and spectrum when it abruptly
terminates its current or scheduled transmission and disrupts a communication cycle. The proposed
project will investigate the spectral and energy impact of a cognitive-radio physical layer on the upper
layers, and propose new network architectures and protocols to reduce or avoid such impact for
improving spectral and energy efficiency in dynamic spectrum access.
Intellectual Merit:
The proposed project investigates cross-layer collaboration for improving spectral and energy efficiency
in dynamic spectrum access. Although the basic approach of cross-layer design is not new in
communications and networking research, the coupling of spectrum access assistance with state
conservation across layers is a new method for improving spectral and energy efficiency in dynamic
spectrum access. In the implementation of this new method, new network architectures and protocols will
need to be investigated, and new insights will be discovered in dynamic spectrum access in terms of
spectral and energy efficiency.
Broader Impacts:
The proposed project will benefit both the society and underrepresented minority groups in STEM.
Spectrum and energy are two types of resources that are critical to a modern society. The limited
spectrum resource becomes more strained every day, while pollution from energy production or
consumption causes serious problems for the environment. The proposed project will improve both
spectral and energy efficiency in wireless networks which are becoming ubiquitous. Global public Wi-Fi
hotspots have been growing at a high speed in recent years, while global Wi-Fi traffic has been growing
even more rapidly than other IP traffic. With the fast growing Wi-Fi traffic, the proposed project will
save billions of kWh of electricity a year in the future because of improved energy efficiency in Wi-Fi
networks. The saved energy will reduce the CO2 equivalent emissions by tens of thousands of tons a year
from reduced electricity generation. The reduced emissions, meanwhile, will have the potential to save
hundreds of human lives and prevent thousands of serious illnesses a year. Besides its likely significant
impact on the society, the project will promote STEM education among minority groups with its hiring
and training of underrepresented minority students in STEM. The majority of the students at UTRGV are
Hispanics, who are underrepresented in STEM. We will actively recruit Hispanic students in the project.
Our recruiting efforts will be facilitated by the resources available at UTRGV, such as the ADVANCE
program funded by NSF and the Office of Engaged Scholarship & Learning, both of which promote
STEM education for Hispanics.

CONGRANT.TITLE: RET site: Research Experiences for Teachers in Embedded Systems Engineering
“RET site: Research Experiences for Teachers in Embedded Systems Engineering,
Data Collection and Transmission for Large-scale and Long-lasting Soil Monitoring (Intent Letter)
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Soils are fundamental resources for humanity and economic prosperity. It is essential for the human to
understand soil processes and maintain the health of soils, otherwise food production cannot be sustained and
living environment can become hostile. One key to maintaining soil health is the ability to monitor the soil in a
large geographic area and for a long time.
To obtain accurate and timely soil measurements in a large geographic area for a long time, wireless
underground sensor networks (WUSN) are likely the only feasible method. It is impractical for wired soil
sensors to cover a large geographic area. Not only are the wires connecting wired soil sensors difficult to
deploy, but also they may easily become interference to the use of the soil. On the other hand, remote sensing
such as satellite imaging provides no or inaccurate data for many soil measurements.
Wireless soil sensors are much easier and cheaper to deploy than wired sensors, and they can also
provide accurate soil measurements. However, when wireless sensors transmit frequently, their life spans will
be short because frequent wireless transmissions drain their batteries quickly. This is particularly true for
underground soil sensors because an underground wireless channel introduces high signal attenuation while
offering little bandwidth [1][2].

CONGRANT.TITLE: A Smart Campus Testbed (Internal PreProposal for NSF MRI)
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The Internet of Things (IoT) is an emerging area that has a big potential of greatly improving the efficiency of our society and also greatly facilitating the daily life of everyone, particularly the seniors and the disabled [7]. However, the implementation and deployment of IoT has been slow. One main reason is that there is a lack of experimental studies on how the heterogeneous IoT elements in reality would interact and interfere with each other in terms of communications, data sharing, and data use [6]. We propose to build an IoT testbed on the UT-RGV campus to do such studies and thus catalyze the acceptance and adoption of IoT by our community and the society. One of UT-RGV’s goals is to broaden our connections to the local communities. The proposed IoT testbed will contribute to achieving that goal because the testbed will attract the attention and
interest of public administrators, teachers, and the general public. The proposed testbed also meets the intellectual merit and the broader impact requirements of NSF, as detailed later.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Sub-Project Title: Priority in Spectrum Use for Networks of Biological Sensors Supporting Time Critical Response (Internal Proposal)
CONGRANT.SPONORG: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) DHS Science and Technology Directorate (S&T) Center of Excellence (COE) Center for Cross-Border Threat Screening and Supply Chain Defense – Center Lead
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: One key in fast response to biological threats is to detect any threat quickly and report it quickly. Any delay in detecting or reporting a threat may result in irreversible consequences. DHS is funding numerous efforts to develop sensors for biological detection. When these sensors are deployed widely on or around the borders, they have to be networked for quickly reporting positive detection. In the scenario of an emergency of biologic detection, one challenge is to make sure that the sensor or sensors detecting the threat be able to have the highest priority in using the spectrum for reporting the detection data without delay. One technique that can be studied for this purpose is  cognitive radio. Cognitive radios are able to adapt their operating parameters, such as frequency, power, and modulation, to the radio environment they constantly sense. When sensors and other nodes sharing the spectrum are equipped with cognitive radios, they become intelligent in using the spectrum and thus can be designed to yield to sensors detecting biologic threats. In this project we plan to study how cognitive radios can be applied in networks of biologic sensors so that sensors detecting threats will have the highest priority in using the spectrum and report the detection without being delayed. We already have some research results on cognitive radio networks and thus are prepared and qualified to conduct the project.

CONGRANT.TITLE: The Impact of a Cognitive Radio Physical Layer in Combat Cognitive Radio Networks
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: In this project we investigate the efficient use of the electromagnetic spectrum in naval combat and the impact of the physical layer change on  the  upper layers. To achieve information dominance, one key is the ability to innovatively use the electromagnetic spectrum in various areas such as surveillance, communications, and navigation. Cognitive radio (CR) has been proposed as an innovative way to improve spectrum efficiency. CRs are expected to be able to adapt their operating parameters, such as frequency, power, and modulation, to the radio environment they constantly sense. In combat there are priority tiers in using the spectrum, and thus some users may be assigned as the primary users, while some others will be the secondary users, as in the case of dynamic spectrum access of cognitive radios. In dynamic spectrum access, secondary users adopting cognitive radios share the spectrum with the primary users. Equipped with cognitive radios, the secondary users can determine at a given time if the primary users are actively using the spectrum. When the primary users are active, the secondary users back off. However, when the primary users are inactive, the secondary users can share the spectrum. In this way the spectrum can be used not only efficiently but also with priority enforced, which will likely be key for information dominance in future naval combat.  Since in combat we still want the secondary user network to be effective, one important question in this scenario of cognitive radio networks is how the cognitive radio physical layer would impact on the secondary user network as a whole. We propose the abstracted network concept in cognitive radio networks and the use of a Markov chain model in analyzing the impact of the primary users on the secondary user network as a whole.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Loyal Robots in Combat
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: One of the main goals of the Robotics Collaborative Technology Alliance is to transfer robots from tools to team members in combat.  Major research efforts have been done to attain the skills of thinking, looking, moving, talking, and working for combat robots so that they can collaborate with soldiers in complex situations. There have been significant successes in these efforts, as shown by recent public demonstrations. It is almost sure that future combat robots will be able to act like soldiers in many of these aspects. However, how to ensure the loyalty of future powerful, and likely dangerous, combat robots is still a big challenge.
